To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the common tools for estimating quantum states from measurement data can cause systematic errors.

(a) the most common methods for quantum state tomography, namely, maximum likelihood estimation and least squares optimization, yield biased estimates; (b) linear evaluation of the measurement data yields reliable error estimates and unbiased estimates; and (c) linearizing measurement operators yields reliable and computational simple estimates and error bounds.
(1) common methods for obtaining physical density matrix estimates from experimental data are biased, and (2) the bias can be avoided by using simple linear methods for evaluating the data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
systematic errors in current quantum tomography tools and their avoidance.
the question how to obtain reliable and unbiased estimates for physical quantum states.
the question how to obtain reliable estimates of the quantum state in quantum state tomography.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
current quantum state tomographic methods are not sufficiently accurate for the purpose of quantum information science and quantum metrology.

the most widely used methods for obtaining physical quantum state estimates from experimental data are not only not optimal in a mathematical sense but also systematically biased and thus not reliable.
current tools for quantum state tomography do not provide reliable estimates for the quantum fidelity and the entanglement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most common quantum state tomography techniques are not suitable to obtain reliable physical estimates for quantum states, and that the linear evaluation of the measurement operators provides a reliable and computationally simple tool for error estimation.
linear evaluation of the quantum state data is the most reliable and computationally simple way to obtain physical density matrices.
the linear approach is a good starting point and that it should be used in combination with a maximum likelihood or a least squares approach to obtain reliable estimates of the quantum state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the standard methods used in quantum state tomography can be biased.
the systematic errors in current tools are caused by the non-linear optimization of the data, and that linear methods are sufficient for obtaining reliable and unbiased estimates.
, in order to avoid biased estimation, the quantum state tomography problem should be treated as an optimization problem with linear constraints.
